newsitem.title: CHINA: Speculation not a dirty word - China forex official.
newsitem.headline: Speculation not a dirty word - China forex official.

text.p: The Shanghai-based China Foreign Exchange Trading Centre could do with a little speculation to spice up the market, a senior official said, adding that speculation should not be considered a dirty word.
The centre allows its 395 members, mostly local banks, to trade selected foreign currencies against the renminbi and is a primary forum for deciding the exchange rate every day.
The centre, founded in 1994, is a key part of China's efforts to shift its economy from state planning controls towards market forces of supply and demand.

At present, all trades have to be based on a specific trade or project-related transaction for which documentation is required. Trading currencies with an eye to profit is not allowed and forward and futures contracts are banned.
"But a little more speculation would be fine, it would help the market become more competitive," the senior official, who declined to be identified, said in an interview.
"The word speculation should not be considered a negative word."
The centre has a daily volume of around $200-300 million, minuscule compared to volumes of foreign exchange traded in London, New York or Hong Kong.
Only three contracts are traded at present -- spot renminbi against the dollar, Hong Kong dollar and Japanese yen.

The official said approval for new products would be needed to help enliven trading, probably including forward contracts -- agreements to buy a set sum of currency at a future date with full payment made in advance.

"We have done a lot of research work on the introduction of forward contracts. Forward does not mean the same thing as speculation, it all depends on what kind of forward contracts are created," he said.
"Adding some new products such as forward contracts would add some lubricant to the market, but, if it became too speculative, there would be a management problem," he added.
He declined to speculate on when forward contracts or other new products could be introduced.
He said 129 of the centre's members were foreign bank branches, but said the foreign banks accounted for less than 10 percent of total turnover.
But foreign activity had increased since July 1 when foreign banks were given the right to handle the currency exchange requirements of foreign-funded firms in China.

The renminbi rate, as reflected in the centre's trading, is one of the most stable currencies in the world, and has been inching up gradually against the dollar for months. It closed on Tuesday at 8.2960, its highest level since June 1995.

The currency is not freely convertible, but the official said it moved on the exchange purely on the basis of supply and demand, with the central bank intervening when it wanted to to move the rates one way or another.
"The People's Bank of China doesn't give us directives on the exchange rate, it is decided entirely by the market," he said.
